transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi... yes, it’s good to meet you too. Thank you for seeing me. 

Well, it’s... it’s actually a bit difficult to articulate, which is frustrating for me because, well, I’m a social worker. I work in mental health and substance abuse, actually, so I’m usually the one sitting in the chair you’re in, trying to help people untangle what they’re experiencing. I have a graduate degree in this, I should be able to just lay it all out clearly, but... when it’s happening to you, it’s just different, isn't it? 

I suppose what finally brought me in today, after putting it off for quite a while, is that I feel like... I feel like the part of me that used to reach out for people has just gone completely quiet. It’s like someone just turned the dial all the way down on my personality. I used to be so deeply engaged with things. I loved my work, I really took pleasure in connecting with my clients and seeing them progress. And outside of work, I was always doing something—I went to Vinyasa yoga three times a week, I’d spend my Saturday afternoons just wandering through different art galleries downtown, looking for new exhibits. I was an avid journaler, too. I have stacks and stacks of notebooks at home filled with thoughts and reflections. 

But lately... I don't know, I just look at my journals and feel absolutely nothing. I haven't been to a gallery in months, and the thought of going to yoga just feels like this impossible mountain to climb. I don't take pleasure in any of it anymore, not even my work, which really scares me given the populations I serve. I’m mostly just... I'm just moving through my obligations. I wake up, I go to work because I have to, I pay my bills, I eat because it's time to eat, but that spark, that drive to actually participate in my life and connect with the world... it's just gone so very quiet. And I just keep waiting for it to come back, but it isn't.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it’s... it’s been a gradual process, but if I really sit down and trace it back, I’d say this whole shift—this change in how I’m thinking, how I’m working, how I’m connecting with people—has been going on for about eight months. 

I remember the timeline pretty clearly because it started right around the time my husband and I took my older relative into our apartment. My aunt, actually. She had a fall, and it just wasn't safe for her to live alone anymore, so we cleared out the guest room and moved her in. And, you know, as a social worker, I thought, "I handle crises all day, I can manage this transition." But having her in our space... it really changed the dynamic of the household. It wasn't just the physical space, it was the emotional space, too. Suddenly, there were all these new routines, new worries, doctor's appointments to coordinate, dietary restrictions to keep track of. 

And I think, at first, I just chalked it up to being tired. You know, caregiver burnout is a very real thing, and I see it in my clients all the time. So I told myself, "Oh, you're just adjusting, you're just exhausted, give it time." But the fatigue never lifted. It just morphed into this... this profound emptiness. The eight months just kind of slipped by, and I kept waiting to bounce back, to find my footing again once we got into a rhythm with my aunt, but instead, I just kept retreating further and further inward. So, yes, about eight months now of just... existing, really.
Do you feel this started because of the stress of your aunt moving in?

Well, that's... that's the tricky part, isn't it? Because on the surface, yes, it makes perfect sense to draw that line. Stress is a massive catalyst, obviously. I tell my own clients that all the time. When you introduce a major life stressor—like a sudden change in caregiving responsibilities, someone moving into your physical space, disrupting your established routines—it's completely natural for the mind to react, sometimes by shutting down. So, intellectually, I look at the timeline and I think, "Okay, Aunt Clara moved in, the stress went up, and then this... this flattening out started." 

But... and this is what really pushed me to finally make an appointment with you... it doesn't feel like just stress. I know what stress feels like. I've been doing this job for over two decades. I've had caseloads that would make your head spin, I've dealt with crises at 2:00 AM, I've had periods of intense burnout where I just wanted to sleep for a week. But this is different. When I was stressed before, I was still... me. I was a tired me, a frustrated me, maybe a slightly irritable me, but the core of who I was remained intact. I still cared, you know? Even when I was exhausted, I still cared about the outcomes. 

Now, with this... it's not that I'm overwhelmed by the stress of my aunt being there. Honestly, my husband has taken on a huge portion of the day-to-day care. He's been wonderful. It's more like... the stress was maybe just a doorway, or a trigger, but what walked through that door isn't just a reaction to her being in the house. It's like the mechanism inside me that processes stress, or joy, or anything at all, is just broken. So, did it start because of the stress? Maybe the timing aligns, but the actual substance of what I'm experiencing... it feels so much deeper and more structural than just caregiver fatigue. It feels like something fundamental has shifted, regardless of whether she's in the guest room or not. I just... I can't quite blame it all on the situation, even though I wish I could, because then there would be a clear solution, right? Just fix the situation. But I don't think fixing the situation would fix... this.
If your aunt were no longer living with you, do you think you would still feel this same emptiness?

I've thought about that a lot, actually. And... yes. Yes, I honestly do think I would still feel this way. 

Because if I really sit with that hypothetical—if my husband and I packed up her things tomorrow and she went to live somewhere else—the physical space in the apartment would open up, sure. The daily schedule would open up. But... well, like I was trying to explain earlier about what finally pushed me to swallow my pride and come in to see you... it’s that the part of me that used to reach out for people, that used to take actual pleasure in things, has just gone so very quiet. And I really don't think her leaving would magically turn the volume back up. 

I mean, I look at my life before all this started, and I was so deeply engaged. I’d be at the clinic, fully invested in my work and my clients, and then I’d be off to Vinyasa yoga to sweat out the day, or I'd be spending my weekends wandering through those downtown galleries, or just sitting at home on the sofa filling up my journals. I had this whole rich, vibrant internal and external life. I was a participant in my own life. 

But now? Even if the house were completely empty and silent, I know I’d still just
Before these past eight months, have you ever had another period in your life when you felt depressed or lost interest in things for at least two weeks?

No... no, actually. And I think that’s part of what makes this whole experience so incredibly baffling to me. If I look back over my life—my twenties, my thirties, most of my forties—I’ve really never had a stretch like this. I mean, sure, I’ve had bad days. We all have bad days, right? You get a terrible cold, or a client's case falls apart, or you're just feeling a little blue because it's February and it's been raining for a week straight. But two whole weeks of just... nothing? Of losing interest in the things that make me who I am? No. Never. 

I've always been, I don't know, the resilient one, I guess. Even back in grad school, when we were all pulling these ridiculous all-nighters and surviving on terrible diner coffee and sheer panic about our clinical practicums, I was always the one organizing the study groups and keeping morale up. I never lost my drive. And then in my career... well, working in mental health and substance abuse, you see a lot of heavy things. You absorb a lot of secondary trauma, so you really have to be hyper-aware of your own emotional baseline. I’ve always been so vigilant about checking in with myself, asking, "Am I getting cynical? Am I burning out?" 

But whenever I felt even a little drained in the past, I always bounced back. A weekend of rest, maybe going to a yoga retreat, or just spending a Saturday reading on the couch, and I was right back in it, fully engaged and ready to go by Monday morning. So, no, I’ve never had a period where the color just drained out of everything for weeks on end like this. This is completely unprecedented for me. It’s... it's like I’m navigating completely uncharted territory, which is frankly terrifying for someone who usually has a map and a treatment plan for absolutely everything.
For most of the past eight months, have you felt down or depressed?

Well, that's... that's the interesting thing about all this, and honestly, it's a distinction I've been trying to parse out in my own head for months now. Because if you ask me if I feel depressed—like, classically depressed, the way we usually define it clinically with the profound sadness, the tearfulness, that heavy, aching feeling in your chest—I'd have to say no. I don't feel sad. I don't sit around crying or feeling this overwhelming sense of despair or hopelessness about the future. 

It's... it's not a presence of a negative emotion, if that makes sense. It's more like an absence. I wouldn't use the word "down" or "depressed" because those words imply that there's a feeling there, even if it's a bad one. What I'm experiencing is just... flat. It's like the emotional bandwidth I used to have has just been completely dialed down to zero. I can look at a situation that should make me feel sad, or a situation that should make me feel happy, and I just feel... neutral. Blank. 

So, no, I haven't been walking around for the last eight months feeling depressed or down in the dumps. It's almost like I wish I did feel sad, because at least sadness is a feeling, you know? At least sadness means you're still connecting with something, that something still matters enough to make you hurt. But this is just a void. It's an emptiness. It's not depression, it's just... nothing. And that nothingness has been there pretty much every day, all day, for this entire eight-month stretch. It's exhausting in its own strange way, just being so completely devoid of any emotional resonance, but no, I wouldn't call it feeling depressed.
For at least six months, have you been worrying excessively about a number of different things in your life?

Well, no. No, I haven't. And honestly, that kind of ties right back into what I was just trying to explain about the emptiness. Because if you really break down what worry actually is... it requires energy, doesn't it? It requires a certain level of emotional investment in how things are going to turn out. You have to care deeply about the future to worry about it. And since I've just been feeling so completely flat, I haven't really been worrying about much of anything. 

Which is incredibly strange for me, because normally, given my line of work and my family situation, I'd have a very healthy amount of everyday stress. I used to be the kind of person who would lie awake at night running through my caseload, wondering if I missed a red flag with a substance abuse client, or fretting about whether my husband and I were saving enough for retirement, or stressing over whether I was managing my aunt's care properly. Just the normal, everyday things that keep responsible people up at night. I was always very conscientious, maybe even a little prone to overthinking things if I'm being completely honest with myself. I liked to have all my bases covered.

But over these last six or eight months? Nothing. My husband could come to me right now and tell me the roof is caving in or our bank account is overdrawn, and I know—intellectually, logically—that I should be concerned. I should feel that familiar knot of anxiety in my stomach, that little spike of adrenaline that tells you to fix a problem. But I just don't. The thought just kind of lands there and sits, and I don't spin out into those "what if" scenarios at all. It's like my brain just refuses to project into the future to find things to stress about. 

It's actually been very hard on my husband, I think, because he'll be stressed about something and looking for a sounding board, looking for me to share that burden with him like I always used to, and I just can't match his urgency. I just look at him and say, well, we'll figure it out, but without any real feeling behind it. So, no, no excessive worrying. Just that same... pervasive, heavy quiet where the worry used to be.
Has this loss of interest and emotional flatness started to interfere with how well you function at work or at home?

Well, yes... yes, it has. And that is probably the most difficult part of all this for me to swallow, given how much pride I’ve always taken in my competence. 

I mean, I’m still showing up to work. I haven't taken a leave of absence, I haven't been calling out sick. Every morning, I go through the motions—I get up, I get dressed, I drive to the clinic, and I sit at my desk. But the reality of what I'm actually accomplishing when I'm sitting there is a completely different story. In community mental health, you know, we rely so heavily on state and federal funding to keep our programs running, and I have always been the one to spearhead those applications. I've always been meticulous about it. But over these last few months, I’ve actually missed grant deadlines. Plural. I had the dates circled on my calendar, I saw the reminders pop up on my computer screen, and I just... stared at them. I couldn't muster the initiative to compile the data or write the narratives. I just let them pass by, which is so incredibly out of character for me that it honestly shocks me when I think about it logically.

And my supervisor, Sarah—we’ve worked together for over a decade, so she knows my baseline better than anyone—she has definitely noticed. She hasn't formally written me up or anything, which in a way almost feels worse, like she's pitying me. But she has quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. I see it happening in the electronic health record system. The high-acuity folks, the ones who need intensive crisis intervention or have really complex dual diagnoses... she's been reassigning them to the newer social workers. And I can't even be angry with her for doing it, because she has to protect the clients, and it is glaringly obvious to anyone paying attention that I’m just not functioning at my usual level. 

And it spills over into home, too. I'm physically present in the house, but my husband is carrying almost the entire mental load right now. I used to manage the household schedule, the bills, the meal planning, checking in on my aunt... and now I just watch the mail pile up on the kitchen island and I can't bring myself to sort it. It’s like the bridge between knowing what I need to do and actually initiating the action has just completely collapsed. So, yes, it's interfering significantly. I'm basically just a ghost haunting my own life right now, just going through the absolute bare minimum motions.
Over the past eight months, have you been having trouble concentrating?

You know, I’ve actually spent a lot of time analyzing that exact thing lately, just trying to parse out what exactly is failing in my day-to-day processes. And I really don't think it's a concentration issue. It’s... it’s not a problem with focus or attention span. 

When I sit at my desk staring at those grant applications I mentioned earlier, it's not that my mind is wandering off to other things. It's not like my thoughts are racing or I'm getting distracted by the noise in the hallway or losing my train of thought halfway through a sentence. If I actually force my eyes to track across a page of text, I can read it. I can comprehend it perfectly fine. The cognitive machinery—the ability to sustain attention and process information—is still completely intact. 

I can sit through a two-hour clinical supervision meeting and I know exactly what was discussed. I can track with my clients during our sessions—even the lower acuity ones Sarah has me seeing now—I can follow their narratives without zoning out or forgetting what they just said two minutes ago. I'm still mentally present in that regard. 

So it's really important to me to make that distinction, especially given what I do for a living. It’s not an attention deficit. It’s just... the drive to apply that attention is what's missing. If I'm reading a case file, I can focus on the words, but I just don't care about what they mean. The bridge between reading the information and actually doing something with it is where everything breaks down. But the focus itself? No, my concentration has been perfectly fine. It’s just that I’m concentrating on... well, on nothing, really. Just sitting there in that quiet, flat space I described. So, no, I wouldn't say I've had any trouble concentrating.
Over the past eight months, has your appetite changed?

My appetite? No, no, I wouldn't say it's changed. I mean, I'm still eating my normal amounts. 

It’s funny you ask that, because my husband and I were actually just discussing the grocery budget the other day, and I realized my eating habits are probably the one thing that has remained completely static through all of this. I still pack the exact same lunch for work that I have for the last five years—a turkey wrap on whole wheat, a little container of mixed berries, and a handful of almonds. I eat it at my desk right around 12:30, just like clockwork. And for dinner, I still eat whatever he puts in front of me. He's been doing most of the cooking lately, bless him, since I just haven't had the drive to meal prep or plan the week's menus like I used to. 

So the physical sensation of hunger is still there, and the volume of food I'm consuming is exactly the same as it was eight months ago. It's not like I'm starving myself or, you know, stress-eating cartons of ice cream at midnight. I've worn the same size pants for a decade and they still fit perfectly fine. 

But I will say... and I suppose this goes right back to that emotional flatness I was trying to explain earlier... the experience of eating is different now. I used to really savor a good meal. I used to love trying new recipes or going out to that little Italian place downtown for our anniversary and really enjoying the flavors. Now, it's just... entirely mechanical. It's just calories in, calories out. I eat because my stomach growls and, logically, I know a human body requires sustenance to keep the organs functioning and the blood sugar stable. I chew, I swallow, I wash my plate. But the appetite itself, the actual physical drive to eat and the amount I'm taking in? No, that hasn't changed at all. It's just the joy of the food that's missing, if that makes sense? I'm definitely still eating my regular three meals a day.
Over the past eight months, have you been having trouble sleeping?

Well, no, actually. Sleep is... it’s a lot like the appetite thing I just mentioned, honestly. It's remained completely intact. I’ve always been a very structured person when it comes to sleep hygiene. In my field, you know, we preach sleep hygiene to our clients constantly—dark room, cool temperature, no screens an hour before bed—and I’ve always practiced what I preach. 

So every night, right around 10:00 PM, I go through the exact same routine. I wash my face, I brush my teeth, I get into bed. My husband usually reads his Kindle for a bit, but I just turn off my lamp. And I fall asleep quite easily. It takes maybe ten or fifteen minutes, max. I don't lie there tossing and turning, and I don't have racing thoughts keeping me awake—mostly because, like I said, I don't really have that kind of mental energy right now. It's just that same flat, quiet emptiness I described before. 

And I stay asleep, too. I'm not waking up at 3:00 AM staring at the ceiling or having strange dreams or anything like that. I sleep a solid seven to eight hours, and then my alarm goes off at 6:15 AM, and I get up. It's strange, though, because you'd think with how exhausting it feels to just exist right now, to push through that heavy fog every single day just to function at the bare minimum, that my sleep would somehow be disrupted by the stress of it all. But it isn't. It’s just another biological function that’s still ticking along perfectly on schedule. I go to sleep, I wake up, the sun rises, and I just start the whole mechanical process over again. 

So, no, no trouble sleeping at all. I get my hours in. It's just that waking up doesn't bring any sense of refreshment or... or readiness for the day, you know? I'm just physically awake again. But the actual mechanics of sleeping are completely normal.
Over the past eight months, have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy?

Tired? Well, I know I just said a moment ago that I don't wake up feeling refreshed, but I really need to be clear about what I mean by that, because it’s not—I’m not actually tired. I'm not experiencing fatigue or low physical energy. Not at all. 

It’s so interesting you ask about energy levels right after sleep, because in my line of work, you know, we see fatigue all the time. Clients come into the clinic and they can barely lift their limbs, they talk about feeling like they're moving through molasses, that profound physical exhaustion. But for me? No, my physical energy is completely baseline. 

My husband actually thought that was the issue at first. He kept saying, you know, "You're just burned out, you've been carrying too heavy a caseload, you're just exhausted." And I had to keep explaining to him that it's not fatigue! I don't need a nap. I don't feel physically drained at the end of the day. I still walk our golden retriever, Buster, for forty-five minutes every single morning before I commute to the clinic. I can carry all the groceries in from the car without feeling winded. My body has plenty of energy. The cellular energy, the physical stamina, it's all firing exactly as it always has. 

It's really more like... well, it’s like having a car with a completely full tank of gas, but the ignition switch is just gone. The fuel is there. The energy is there. I have all the physical capacity in the world to do things, I just don't have the... the spark to initiate them. That drive we were talking about earlier. But if you were to measure my actual energy output, or my physical tiredness? Completely normal. I don't have heavy limbs, I don't feel lethargic, I'm not dragging myself around. I just sit there in that quiet space because I have no internal reason to move, not because I lack the energy to do so. 

So, I really wouldn't classify it as being low on energy. The energy is definitely there, just sort of... sitting in a vacuum, I suppose. So no, no unusual tiredness.
Over the past eight months, have other people noticed that you’ve been moving or speaking more slowly than usual?

Well, no... no, nobody has said anything like that. Moving or speaking slowly... no. 

It’s funny, because my husband—who, as I might have mentioned, has been hovering a bit lately, watching me like a hawk to see if I'm getting worse or better—he hasn't brought up anything about my pace. And believe me, if I were shuffling around the house or taking five minutes to answer a simple question, he would be the first to point it out and probably try to schedule me an appointment with a neurologist or something. But no, my physical movements are just as brisk as they’ve always been. Like I said about walking the dog, my stride is exactly the same. I don't drag my feet, I don't move like I'm underwater. 

And as for my speech, well, you can probably tell just from sitting here with me, I still talk at a pretty normal clip. In my line of work, especially when doing intake assessments at the clinic or running case consultations with the other social workers, you have to be able to keep the conversation moving. You have to guide the dialogue and keep things on track. And I haven't had any trouble with that. I don't lose my train of thought halfway through a sentence or take these long, drawn-out pauses before I respond to a client. My articulation, the actual speed of the words coming out of my mouth, is completely unchanged. 

I think it really goes back to what I was trying to articulate about the energy levels. The hardware is fine, you know? The engine runs at the exact same speed it always has. I might not feel compelled to start a conversation—I'm perfectly content to just sit in silence at the dinner table because I just don't have the urge to chat about how the day went or gossip about the neighbors—but if my husband asks me a question about the mortgage or what we need from the grocery store, I answer him right away, at my normal speed. So, no, no one has noticed any sluggishness or slowing down, and I haven't felt anything like that either. The mechanics of my movement and my speech are completely intact.
Over the past eight months, have you been feeling worthless or excessively guilty?

Worthless? Guilty? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. 

It’s actually quite the opposite, in a strange way. You know, in my practice, I see a lot of guilt. I see clients who feel like absolute burdens to their families, people who are just consumed by shame over past mistakes or how they're handling their current struggles. They have this heavy, crushing sense of worthlessness that just eats away at them, and they cry in my office, and they apologize for taking up space. I know intimately what that looks like. I've spent years sitting across from it. 

But for me? That is completely absent. Because guilt... well, guilt requires a certain level of emotional engagement, doesn't it? You have to actually care about the expectations you feel you're failing to meet, or you have to feel some sort of sharp, internal emotional pain about your place in the world. And as I've been trying to explain with the energy and the sleep, I just don't have that emotional resonance right now. The tank is empty in that regard. 

I don't sit around thinking I'm a bad wife to my husband because I don't want to chat at dinner, or a bad social worker because I'm just going through the mechanical motions of my job at the clinic. I just... am. I exist. There's no value judgment attached to it in my head whatsoever. I'm not beating myself up over this state of being, because to beat yourself up, you have to feel that you deserve punishment, and I don't feel that either. It's just this profound, quiet neutrality. 

My husband actually struggles to understand this part. He’ll sometimes try to reassure me, saying things like, "It's okay that you're not yourself right now, please don't feel bad about it." And I have to look at him and explain, again, that I *don't* feel bad about it. Which I think confuses him even more, to be honest. I think he expects me to be grieving my loss of passion or feeling terribly guilty for being so disconnected from our marriage and our life, but the truth is, I don't feel guilty at all. I don't feel worthless, I don't feel exceptionally valuable... I just don't feel much of anything on that spectrum. The emotional weight of guilt just isn't there to carry. So, no, I haven't been dealing with anything like that.
Over the past eight months, have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living?

Life not being worth living? No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. 

I know that’s a standard question—we ask it all the time during intake assessments at the clinic, it’s right there on the risk assessment forms, usually right after asking about hopelessness or despair. And I know why you have to ask it, because when someone describes this profound lack of motivation, this total absence of joy or connection to their daily life, the logical clinical leap is to assume they must be profoundly depressed and contemplating whether life is even worth continuing. It’s a very common trajectory for many of the people I see professionally. They lose their spark, and then they start wondering what the point of it all is, and then they start having those dark thoughts.

But for me, it’s completely different. It’s almost... well, it’s almost entirely devoid of that kind of existential dread. I don't sit in my living room, staring at the wall, thinking that life is meaningless or that I'd be better off not being here. The concept of life being "worth living" implies a sort of value judgment, a weighing of the pros and cons of existence, and as I was saying about the guilt, I'm just not operating in a space where I'm making those kinds of evaluations right now. 

I'm not in pain. That's the thing my husband really struggles to grasp. He sees me so detached, so indifferent to the things we used to enjoy—like our weekend trips to the coast, or even just sitting on the patio with a glass of wine—and he assumes I must be suffering terribly inside. He’ll ask me, "Are you in a dark place? Are you having bad thoughts?" And I have to explain to him, over and over, that it's not dark. It's not light, either. It's just... neutral. It's a flatline. 

To have thoughts that life isn't worth living, you have to feel a sense of anguish, or a desperate desire to escape from something intolerable. But my current state isn't intolerable to me. It's just empty. I wake up, I take Buster for his walk, I go to the clinic, I listen to my clients, I come home, I eat dinner. I go through the motions of living without any internal friction. I don't feel a desire to end it, just as I don't feel a burning passion to engage with it. I'm just here, existing, day by day. 

So, no, I haven't had any suicidal ideation, no thoughts of death, no feeling that life is a burden I want to put down. It's just... happening around me, and I'm present for it, even if I'm not really participating in it the way I used to.
Over the past eight months, have you found yourself thinking a lot about death, even if you haven’t wanted to harm yourself?

Thinking about death... no. No, not at all. 

It really just ties right back into what I was just saying about those questions on the risk assessments. Death is... well, death is a very heavy, philosophically dense concept, isn't it? When people think a lot about death—and I see this all the time with my substance abuse clients, or the ones dealing with severe, complicated grief—they're usually doing it because they're terrified of it, or they're obsessed with the legacy they're leaving behind, or they're just hyper-fixated on the fragility of everything. There's a tremendous amount of emotional and cognitive energy required to sit and ponder mortality. You have to be deeply invested in the concept of life, or at least deeply disturbed by it, to spend your time ruminating on its end. 

And as I've been saying, I just don't have that kind of investment or energy right now. I'm not reading obituaries or wondering what happens after we die. I'm not having existential crises while I'm walking Buster around the block. 

It's funny, my husband actually probed around this topic a few weeks ago. We were watching some documentary on television, and a prominent figure in it passed away, and my husband kept looking over at me. I could feel him doing it, trying to gauge my reaction, watching to see if it triggered something in me. He eventually paused it and asked if it bothered me, or if my current state of mind made me think about my own mortality more often. And I had to tell him, honestly, it just didn't register on that level. I recognize death as a biological fact, obviously, but I don't spend any time dwelling on it. 

My mind is just... it's very quiet in that regard. There's no morbid fascination, no dwelling on the end of things, no intrusive thoughts about the grave. It's just the day-to-day routine. Getting up, going to the clinic, doing my intakes, coming home. Those grand, sweeping human concepts like death and legacy and mortality... they just don't occupy any space in my head these days. It takes too much bandwidth, and I'm just operating on a very simple, neutral baseline. So, no, I haven't been preoccupied with death in the slightest.
During these past eight months, have there been days when you felt sad?

Sad? No... no, I really haven't. It’s... well, it’s exactly like what I was just saying about the guilt and the thoughts of death. Sadness is an active emotion, isn't it? When I see clients at the clinic who are sad—and I mean truly, deeply sad—there is a palpable weight to them. You can see it in their posture, in the way they cry, the way their voice catches when they talk about what they've lost. They are actively mourning something, even if it’s just their own loss of joy. They feel the absence of happiness as a sharp, painful thing. I know what that looks like. I'm trained to look for it. But I don't have that. 

My husband, bless his heart, he really struggles with this distinction. He keeps looking for the sadness in me. He’ll buy me flowers, or he’ll suggest we go out to that little Italian place we used to love, and when I just say, 'No thank you, I'd rather just stay in,' I can see his face fall. He thinks I'm sitting on the couch wrapped in a blanket because I'm just so overwhelmed with sorrow. He thinks I'm holding it all in, trying to be brave or something. And I've tried to explain to him, I'm not crying when he leaves the room. I'm not holding back tears. There's no lump in my throat. I'm literally just sitting there.
